hook: Hundreds of feet of water once stood where this hotel is.
text: Hundreds of feet of water once stood where this hotel is. Where Zion Lodge sits today, the lake was about three hundred and fifty to three hundred and eighty feet deep. A mountainside fell, dammed the river, and the lake slowly filled with mud. Full documentary: The Day the Mountain Fell, on YouTube.

About a minute. That's how long it took a mountainside to fall into Zion Canyon, about four thousand eight hundred years ago. Models suggest the rock averaged about a hundred and twelve miles per hour and peaked near two hundred. The main mass crossed the canyon in about twenty seconds. One geologist who studied it called it a minute with up to ten thousand years of consequences. Here's why. Watch The Day the Mountain Fell on our channel.

Ninety Hoover Dams. That's how much concrete you'd need to rebuild the mountainside that collapsed into Zion Canyon. About ten billion cubic feet of rock, roughly five times bigger than any landslide in North America's recorded history, not counting volcanoes. The full story: The Day the Mountain Fell, on our YouTube channel.

hook: About four hundred and thirty people cut off, and one road gone.
text: About four hundred and thirty people cut off, and one road gone. On the night of April twelfth, nineteen ninety-five, part of an ancient landslide in Zion moved again. It blocked the Virgin River, and the river cut a new path straight through the road. About six hundred feet of it was destroyed. Guests and employees at Zion Lodge were stuck. Crews carved an emergency detour out of the canyon wall in about twenty-two hours. Full documentary: The Day the Mountain Fell, on YouTube.

hook: Two hundred and sixty-five thousand board feet of lumber, down a wire.
text: Two hundred and sixty-five thousand board feet of lumber, down a wire. That's how Zion Lodge was built in nineteen twenty-five. A tramway on Cable Mountain lowered the wood more than two thousand vertical feet to the canyon floor. Watch The Day the Mountain Fell on our channel.

hook: Three thousand feet up, a slab of sandstone let go.
text: Three thousand feet up, a slab of sandstone let go. August twenty-fourth, twenty nineteen: rock broke off Cable Mountain, above Weeping Rock. More than four hundred and thirty-five thousand cubic feet of debris came down. Three visitors were hurt. Part of a trail was buried under what geologists called a small rock avalanche. The twist? Nearly a century earlier, that same mountain had lowered the lumber for Zion Lodge on a wire. The full story is in The Day the Mountain Fell, on YouTube.

A hundred and eight days. On January twenty-sixth, nineteen sixty-six, the main building of Zion Lodge burned. A prefabricated replacement was up and operating a hundred and eight days later. And all of it stands on the bed of an ancient lake. Full documentary: The Day the Mountain Fell.

hook: Fewer than eighty deer became six hundred.
text: Fewer than eighty deer became six hundred. Two Oregon State ecologists argue that when crowds pushed the cougars out of Zion Canyon in the nineteen thirties, the deer boomed. Between nineteen thirty-eight and nineteen forty-seven, the Park Service killed or removed seven hundred and eighty of them. And the deer ate the young cottonwoods. In nearby North Creek, where cougars stayed, the researchers found almost forty times more young trees. It's a debated idea. Watch The Day the Mountain Fell on our YouTube channel.

hook: Five thousand tons of rock, and no visitor killed.
text: Five thousand tons of rock, and no visitor killed. In nineteen sixty-eight, a rockfall that size hit the end of the trail to the Narrows. In Zion, rocks fall often. Yet according to the Park Service, no visitor has ever died from one here. Full documentary: The Day the Mountain Fell, on our channel.

hook: A lake that lasted seven hundred years, then filled itself in.
text: A lake that lasted seven hundred years, then filled itself in. When a mountainside fell into Zion Canyon, it dammed the Virgin River, and a lake some call Lake Zion filled the valley. Then the river slowly buried it, dropping sand and mud into the still water, until about four thousand one hundred years ago the lake was full. Not of water. Of sediment. That's the flat floor of Zion Canyon today. Full documentary: The Day the Mountain Fell, on YouTube.
